title: How AI Can Prevent Claims from Aging into the 60-, 90-, and 120-Day Buckets
summary: The 60-to-90-day AR window should be treated as an early-warning zone where AI can identify payer and internal patterns before claims become deeply aged.
body_markdown:
*The 60-to-90-day window should be an early-warning zone, not simply another work queue*


**By Vanessa Couch-Laguana, Head of RCM, LunaBill**


---


The 60-to-90-day bucket is not just old AR. It is a window in which emerging payer and internal patterns can still be corrected.


## Do not wait for old AR to become a crisis


Ideally, many claims should pay within 30 days. In practice, an average closer to 45 days may be more realistic depending on payer and contract. Once a clean, accepted claim reaches 60 days without payment, leaders should begin asking why. The period between 60 and 90 days is where patterns can still be identified before the account becomes deeply aged.


The problem is capacity. Leaders often do not have enough time or analytical support to review that bucket in a meaningful way. Teams continue to work high-dollar lists and individual accounts, but no one steps back to examine what happened between bill date, acceptance date, expected payment date, and the present status.


## Treat 60 to 90 days as a pattern-detection window


The review should segment claims by payer, denial or status, specialty, facility, and relevant contract term. Leaders should look at payment behavior, the age of the oldest affected claim, the highest-dollar exposure, and whether comparable claims have already paid. They should also compare expected reimbursement with actual payment behavior rather than using one broad assumption across every payer.


The objective is to identify a change early: a payer that has begun delaying clean claims, a recurring authorization gap, a claim-status response that is not being converted into the right next action, or an internal workflow that is holding charges or documentation.


## Prevention begins before the claim exists


Aging prevention is not only a back-end follow-up strategy. Accurate insurance information, coordination of benefits, eligibility, patient estimates, authorization, charge capture, coding, signed documentation, and clean-claim edits all influence whether the account will age.


Technology should trigger the right work while the patient is still receiving care. A change in level of care, an extended stay, or an added procedure should route to the appropriate clinical work queue with a defined service-level expectation. If information can be submitted through a portal automatically, that should occur while the clinical team is still available to intervene. Waiting until discharge pushes the problem into billing, where it becomes harder and more expensive to resolve.


## Use AI to turn data into timely action


Revenue Cycle teams have enormous amounts of data. The challenge is using it to work smarter. AI can call out unusual aging patterns, connect them with payer and contract behavior, summarize the affected volume and dollars, and recommend the next action before leaders have to manually assemble the story.


It should also help distinguish between an account that needs routine follow-up and a population that should be escalated as a systemic issue. That allows leaders to stop spending human time on repetitive work and focus on the internal correction, payer conversation, or clinical decision that will prevent the next group of claims from aging.


## AI is a tool—and leaders still own the outcome


After 29 years in Revenue Cycle operations, the most important message I can offer is that AI is a tool. Used well, it can remove some of the anxiety and legwork that keep leaders up at night. It can supplement the team, enhance daily work, and help systems work for us rather than against us.


AI will not eliminate internal process problems or the need for executive and clinical support. It will not replace judgment where contract interpretation, medical necessity, or specialized investigation is required. But it can make the right issues visible sooner and leave more value-added work with the people best qualified to perform it.


I spent more than half my life in Revenue Cycle operations. I would not have moved into this side of the industry if I did not genuinely believe in what the technology can do. The opportunity is not to automate for the sake of automation. It is to help leaders and teams focus on the right actions at the right time.
